newsitem.title: INDIA: INVESTORS CHOOSY AS MORE INDIAN BANKS GO PUBLIC.
newsitem.headline: INVESTORS CHOOSY AS MORE INDIAN BANKS GO PUBLIC.

text.p: Bank shares have become front runners on Indian stock markets since a 1993 public issue by the State Bank of India (SBI), but investors are becoming increasingly selective as more banks go public.
Four other public sector banks have floated their shares, and most of them are actively traded and quoted at a premium over offer prices.
"But we are going to see an oversupply of banking paper," said Abhay Modi, banking analyst at Lloyds Securities.
"Investors are going to become choosy. It is already evident as some private banks in the south are only quoting at multiples three to four times their earnings."
Investors are now more discriminating in picking bank scrips, brokers and fund managers said.
The current favourites are SBI, Bank of Baroda and Bank of India among public sector banks, and HDFC Bank among private banks.
"We would recommend SBI and HDFC Bank to investors looking for good buys over a longer horizon," said Manish, an analyst at SSKI Securities.
The older private sector banks such as Federal Bank and the recently listed state-run Dena Bank are no longer fancied as brokerages recommend larger, healthier banks.
SBI, the industry's giant with more than 8,000 branches and 232,000 employees, is still the hottest choice among Indian and foreign funds.
But foreign institutional investors (FIIs) have been banned from making fresh purchases of SBI after FIIs' aggregate holding touched a 20 percent ceiling imposed by law.

Investors lapped up SBI's public issue in late 1993 -- the first public share issue by an Indian bank -- as it offered an exposure to the entire economy unlike shares of manufacturing firms whose price movements can track cyclical troughs.

An analyst at a European investment bank said SBI's price-earning ratio of 13.7 times 1996/97 (April-March) earnings was above Bank of Baroda's 13.5, Bank of India's 11.6 and Oriental Bank of Commerce's 7.5.
"SBI's premium to its peers is justified due to its higher fee based income, better management, sector dominance, hidden reserves and stronger liquidity on bourses," the analyst said.

New private banks which have sprung up since 1994 when the government allowed their entry into the industry account for a fraction of the industry's market capitalisation of about 20 billion rupees ($560 million).
The private banks enjoy the benefits of high technology and are fast growing, but the lack of a countrywide retail reach is a major disadvantage, analysts said.
Securities firms and mutual funds are eagerly awaiting the initial public offering of Corporation Bank in September.

Beyond September, investors are eyeing Canara Bank and Punjab National Bank, two well-known public sector brands. But the rest of India's 20-odd public sector banks have a long way to go and need to clean their books before going public, analysts said.
Indian stock markets are now aligning themselves with other markets around the world where the service sector accounts for a major chunk of market capitalisation, they said.

From less than five percent before SBI's 1993 share issue, the finance sector, including banks, housing finance companies and term-lending banks, now accounts for more than 15 percent of total market capitalisation, analysts said.
"The world over, bank stocks dominate markets," Hrikesh Anjaria, an analyst at Khandwala Finance, said. "Bank stocks will perform in tune with the economy and the industry."
Bankers say share issues to employees and the public have made them more accountable and helped the banks become more efficient and competitive.
"This will bring about a total change in the attitude of banks," Bank of Baroda chairman K. Kannan told Seuters.
More than 2,000 shareholders recently attended the bank's first annual general meeting, he said.
"This may be the most significant effect of reforms -- allowing banks to go public and exposing them to demands of shareholders," Kannan said. ($1=35.7 rupees)
